claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature BCC state.
The stability of the initial BCC state is governed primarily by the Gibbs free-energy difference between BCC and FCC phases.
On cooling, ΔG_bcc-fcc shifts sufficiently negative and thereby favors FCC formation.
FCC formation occurs only if kinetic restrictions such as insufficient diffusion do not inhibit transformation.
Slow cooling allows the alloy to approach equilibrium more closely than rapid quenching.
Rapid quenching minimizes transformation by kinetic suppression.
CALPHAD thermodynamic calculations using the cited database are unreliable below approximately 0 °C.
The magnitude and sign of ΔG_bcc-fcc mediate BCC and FCC phase fractions.
ΔG_bcc-fcc provides an energetic threshold for FCC nucleation and growth from BCC.
BCC is stabilized at high temperature in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Cooling increases the thermodynamic instability of BCC relative to FCC.
During slow cooling, atomic diffusion permits FCC to nucleate and grow from the initial BCC microstructure.
Rapid quenching kinetically traps the high-temperature BCC state despite a thermodynamic driving force toward FCC.
Slow-cooled samples will have a higher FCC phase fraction than rapidly quenched samples.
Rapidly quenched samples will remain predominantly BCC.
Measured phase fractions should correlate qualitatively with calculated ΔG_bcc-fcc trends.
Local compositional variations, minor alloying effects, and thermodynamic-database limitations can make quantitative phase fractions and transformation rates uncertain.
Failure of slow cooling to increase FCC fraction relative to quenching would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.

contradictions.description: Rapid quenching is a central comparison for which a specific predominantly-BCC outcome is predicted, but extremely rapid quenching is also declared potentially outside the hypothesis's predictive scope.
